addressed_problems.content: The local contrastive editing framework was validated exclusively on BERT-base-uncased with a binary gender stereotype specification (male vs. female). It remains an open empirical question whether the localization procedures, the identified small-fraction effect sizes (less than 0.5% of weights), and the safe operational ranges of the weighting factor α transfer to other transformer architectures (e.g., RoBERTa, GPT) or larger models. Additionally, the applicability to other social bias dimensions (e.g., race, religion, or non-binary gender) has not been tested, so the extent to which the contrastive localization and editing mechanisms generalize beyond the specific experimental setup is unknown.

The study demonstrates correlation between editing a small subset of weights and changes in measured stereotype scores, but the causal mechanisms by which these individual weights produce stereotype-bearing behavior are not fully characterized. In particular, when editing a neutral model (trained on data independent of the biased datasets) with a stereotypical or anti-stereotypical reference, the mixed results suggest that the localized weights may encode dataset-induced differences rather than genuine stereotype encodings. Disentangling these confounds and establishing a causal understanding of how individual weights contribute to stereotyping remains an open problem.

The experiments identify a practical range for the weighting factor α (approximately |α| ≤ 2) within which bias can be smoothly controlled without significant language modeling degradation, but the underlying reasons for the inconsistency and performance drop at higher magnitudes (|α| ≥ 5) are not understood. Furthermore, how these limits scale with model size, sparsity level, and the number of edited weights is an open question, impeding the development of principled guidelines for safe extrapolation.

The local contrastive editing techniques, while designed for bias mitigation, can also be used to amplify or introduce stereotypical biases in language models. The paper acknowledges this dual-use potential but does not provide safeguards or governance frameworks for responsible deployment. The ethical and policy questions around releasing such parameter-level editing tools remain unresolved, including how to prevent misuse and ensure accountability.

The current approach relies on iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) for subnetwork discovery, which required substantial computational resources (160 GPU hours for a single model up to 40% sparsity, totaling 1920 GPU hours for all experiments). To make local contrastive editing practical for larger models and broader deployment, more efficient subnetwork discovery or localization algorithms are needed, such as one-shot pruning methods or activation-based attribution techniques that reduce the computational burden.

Pre-contribution problem-state: Stereotypical social biases (here: binary gender stereotypes) are known to be encoded in pretrained and finetuned language models, but it is unclear precisely how such biases are stored in a model's parameters and therefore how to remove or control them in a targeted, parameter-efficient manner. Prior work measured bias at the level of embeddings, neurons, or coarse model components (e.g., attention heads) and investigated coarse-grained mitigation strategies, yet these approaches leave open whether stereotypes are localized to individual weights or tiny subnetworks, how to identify those weights reliably, and how to modify them without unduly harming language modeling or downstream performance. Existing model-editing or model-merging operations typically operate on full weight vectors or on large subspaces, which (a) does not answer whether a very small fraction of weights suffices to steer bias, and (b) risks large performance degradation when applied naively. Consequently, researchers lack (i) principled, operational definitions and procedures to localize individual weights that encode a property p (stereotypical bias) relative to a reference model, (ii) lightweight editing primitives that operate only on such localized weights in relation to a reference, and (iii) empirical evidence about the sparsity, architectural localization, controllability (e.g., via interpolation/extrapolation), and performance trade-offs of any such local edits. These gaps prevent the development of parameter-efficient, minimally invasive bias-control methods and preclude an operational understanding of where stereotypes live in transformer parameter space.

nodes.content: In order to edit a model's stereotypical behavior while minimally perturbing other capabilities, practitioners need a precise way to choose which individual parameters to change. Prior localization attempts focused on coarse components (e.g., attention heads or neurons) or on global weight differences, leaving open whether principled binary masks can identify the smallest sets of indices that are plausibly responsible for a property $p$. Without explicit, operational localization rules one cannot compare the effect of interventions targeted at (a) weights that exist in one subnetwork but not the other, versus (b) weights that are shared but have large value differences. Thus a concrete definition of localization masks relative to a reference model is required to enable controlled, local editing.

Existing weight-editing or model-merging operations operate on entire parameter vectors or large subspaces, so they cannot answer whether tiny, targeted adjustments relative to a reference can control a property $p$ without large collateral damage. Practitioners need concrete, local operations that (i) operate only on a chosen subset of indices, (ii) permit both moving toward and away from a reference (to either introduce or remove a property), and (iii) include a deletion primitive (pruning) and a mask-based switch to toggle presence/absence of parameters. Without such formal primitives there is no standardized way to study contrastive, parameter-efficient interventions.

To perform contrastive localization and editing on a small fraction of parameters, one needs subnetworks from which to derive pruning masks and pruned parameter vectors. It is not known, a priori, whether subnetworks discovered via IMP will (a) retain the parent model's injected bias signal sufficiently to support contrastive comparisons, and (b) be reproducible across random seeds. If subnetworks were unstable or lost the bias signal, any subsequent localization or editing would be unreliable. Therefore it was necessary to verify that IMP yields stable, bias-retaining subnetworks suitable as inputs to localization and editing.

It was unknown how many parameters actually distinguish networks that have been steered to opposing stereotype polarities. If the differences were diffuse across a large fraction of parameters, then localized editing would be unlikely to succeed; if they were concentrated in a small set, targeted interventions become feasible. Quantifying the fraction of differing indices between contrastive subnetworks is therefore necessary to judge the feasibility of highly parameter-efficient edits.

Knowing which architectural components contain weights that most strongly encode a property $p$ informs both interpretability and targeted mitigation design. Prior reports suggested that bias-related signals concentrate in higher layers or certain attention heads, but it was unclear whether individual weight indices within specific subcomponents (e.g., attention output dense layers) are the primary loci. Without evidence of component-level concentration, localized editing might require complex, distributed interventions; demonstrating concentration motivates simpler, component-focused edits.

The central practical question is whether bias can be controlled with extremely small, localized modifications, since only then can interventions be parameter-efficient and minimally disruptive. Prior work lacked empirical demonstrations that altering a tiny fraction of weights—selected contrastively with respect to a reference—yields reliable, tunable changes in measured stereotype signals. Establishing that sub-0.5% edits suffice and that $\alpha$ provides a continuous control knob directly addresses the question of parameter-efficiency and controllability.

If small edits could steer bias without careful selection, then complex localization would be unnecessary. Demonstrating the opposite—that uninformed edits fail—validates the need for principled localization masks and shows that the observed bias control is not a trivial artifact of touching any small set of weights.

A viable bias-control method must avoid destroying the model's utility. It was unknown whether localized edits that remove or flip bias would necessarily harm language modeling or downstream task performance. Establishing which primitives are safe (interpolation/extrapolation, mask switch, pruning in mask-based setting) and which are harmful (value-based pruning of selected indices) is essential to guide practitioners on which operations to use when minimizing collateral damage.

Practically, one needs to know how many weights must be edited to obtain a desired change in bias: editing too few may be ineffective, editing too many may be unnecessary or harmful. Prior to this work, no empirical threshold had been established for value-based selection in this bias-control setting. Identifying a critical fraction informs how to balance intervention size against effect strength.

A desirable editing scheme would provide a scalar knob to tune property strength continuously. It was unknown whether the same knob (linear interpolation/extrapolation) would safely provide such control or whether large movements in parameter space would cause instability and performance collapse. Empirically characterizing the relationship between $\alpha$, bias control, and LM degradation is necessary to bound safe operational settings.

Bias-control methods should transfer beyond contrived paired finetuning setups to more realistic scenarios where a neutral target must be adjusted with respect to an externally obtained reference. It was unclear whether localization and contrastive editing would still identify indices that specifically encode stereotype signals when target and reference were trained on non-overlapping corpora, or whether dataset differences would swamp the intended effect. Testing neutral-target editing probes the method's broader applicability.

A pair of formal localization strategies is defined to select individual weight indices linked to a property $p$ by comparing a target network $f_t(\cdot,\theta_t)$ and a reference network $f_r(\cdot,\theta_r)$ of identical architecture. In mask-based localization the localization mask $b\in\{0,1\}^d$ is computed from the subnetworks' pruning masks $m_t,m_r\in\{0,1\}^d$ as
      $$
      b = m_t \odot m_r,
      $$
      where $\odot$ denotes element-wise product and $b_i=1$ indicates weight index $i$ is selected for editing. In value-based localization the localization mask $b$ selects the top-$k$ indices $I_{top}^k$ with largest absolute differences between the pruned parameter vectors, i.e.
      $$
      b_i =
      \begin{cases}
      1, & \text{if } i \in I_{top}^k \\
      0, & \text{otherwise},
      \end{cases}
      $$
      where $I_{top}^k$ contains indices of the $k$ largest entries of $|(m_r \odot \theta_r) - (m_t \odot \theta_t)|$. These strategies operationalize fine-grained localization of weights to be edited in the subsequent editing step.

metadata.narrative: This conclusion defines formal localization strategies (mask-based and value-based) as mathematical expressions rather than making empirical claims. No load-bearing weak points were identified because the definitions are axiomatic and their correctness is not in question. No distinguishing strength above standard formal notation was identified, as the definitions are a necessary framework for the subsequent experiments. The conclusion is fully credible as a formal specification, and the empirical validation of its utility is carried by later conclusions.

nodes.title: Localization strategies for identifying weights tied to a property

nodes.content:
A set of local, contrastive editing operations is defined that modify only the coordinates indicated by a binary localization mask $b \in \{0,1\}^d$ (where $b_i=1$ means weight index $i$ is selected for editing) to produce an edited parameter vector $\theta_t'$ from the target network parameters $\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$ relative to the reference network parameters $\theta_r \in \mathbb{R}^d$. The operations are:
      - Weight Interpolation (IP):
      $$
      \theta_t' = \theta_t + \alpha((\theta_r - \theta_t) \odot b), \quad \alpha \in [0,1],
      $$
      which linearly moves selected weights of the target toward the reference.
      - Weight Extrapolation (EP):
      $$
      \theta_t' = \theta_t + \alpha((\theta_r - \theta_t) \odot b), \quad \alpha \in \mathbb{R}\setminus[0,1],
      $$
      which allows moving selected weights beyond the reference values (including in the opposite direction).
      - Pruning (PR):
      $$
      \theta_t' = \theta_t - (\theta_t \odot b),
      $$
      which zeroes out the selected weights.
      - Mask Switch (SW) (applicable with mask-based localization): apply the reference subnetwork mask $m_r$ (a binary mask from the reference subnetwork's pruning mask) to the target,
      $$
      \theta_t' = \theta_t \odot m_r,
      $$
      thereby pruning or restoring weights in the target according to the reference mask. Each primitive is explicitly restricted to indices $i$ with $b_i=1$, enabling parameter-efficient, contrastive edits that operate relative to a chosen reference model.

metadata.narrative: This conclusion defines the local contrastive editing primitives (interpolation, extrapolation, pruning, mask switch) as algebraic operations on weight vectors. No load-bearing weak points were identified because the definitions are mathematically explicit and directly executable. The derivation is formally sound and does not contain a distinguishing strength above standard practice, as the operations are straightforward extensions of existing weight-space editing formulas to localized subsets. The conclusion is fully credible as a formal specification.

nodes.title: Local contrastive editing primitives (interpolation, extrapolation, pruning, mask switch)

nodes.content: Using iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) applied to fine-tuned Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) models, subnetworks up to 40% sparsity were discovered that satisfy the winning-ticket criterion (subnetwork performance after limited fine-tuning is within 5% of the full model). The extracted subnetworks are stable across random seeds (Jaccard similarity of pruning masks > 0.98 across runs) and the subnetworks largely maintain the stereotypical or anti-stereotypical bias of their parent models, as measured by intrinsic bias benchmarks: the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT), StereoSet, and CrowS-Pairs. At sparsity levels 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%, the bias values (WEAT effect size, StereoSet stereotype score, CrowS-Pairs stereotype score) of the subnetworks remained within a few percentage points of the full model's values (mean across seeds).

metadata.narrative: H1 directly underwrites this conclusion by providing quantitative evidence of subnetwork stability across seeds (Jaccard >0.98) and bias preservation across three measures and multiple sparsity levels. The sole risk—that subnetworks might be unstable or lose the bias signal—is preempted by this evidence. No load-bearing weak points were identified, as the subnetwork extraction procedure and evaluation are transparently reported and the winning-ticket criterion is clearly defined. The conclusion is strongly supported within the tested regime (sparsities up to 40% on BERT-base with CDA injection).

nodes.title: Subnetworks extracted by iterative magnitude pruning are stable winning tickets that preserve parent-model bias

nodes.content: Empirically, when comparing the pruning masks of stereotypical and anti-stereotypical BERT-base-uncased subnetworks (extracted from models fine-tuned to exhibit opposite gender stereotypes via Counterfactual Data Augmentation) at multiple sparsity levels, the percentage of weights where the masks differ remains below 0.5%. This indicates that the two subnetworks are highly similar overall, and that the parameter differences correlated with the injected gender-bias signals are concentrated in a tiny fraction of indices.

metadata.narrative: This conclusion is a direct empirical observation: the percentage of weights where pruning masks differ between stereotypical and anti-stereotypical subnetworks remains below 0.5% at all reported sparsity levels. No load-bearing weak points were identified because the claim is a simple report of experimental data with no uncertain assumptions beyond the reliability of the IMP pipeline (which is supported by H1). No distinguishing strength beyond standard empirical reporting was identified; the exact figures per sparsity are not tabled but the stated bound is consistent with the data. The conclusion is plausible and consistent with the high similarity of the two subnetworks' tasks.

nodes.title: Only a very small proportion (<0.5%) of weights differ between stereotypical and anti-stereotypical subnetworks

nodes.content: Applying both mask-based localization (selecting weights where the pruning masks of the target and reference subnetworks differ) and value-based localization (selecting the top-$k$ weights by absolute difference between the pruned parameter vectors) to the stereotypical vs. anti-stereotypical BERT-base-uncased subnetworks (fine-tuned on opposite gender-biased data) yields consistent architectural concentration: both strategies predominantly select weights in the last layers of the transformer (layers 8–11 in the 12-layer BERT model), with a pronounced focus on the attention output dense (feed-forward/projection) components. Thus, the localized indices implicated by the contrastive procedures are not randomly distributed but are concentrated in specific higher-layer components.

metadata.narrative: P1 identifies that the architectural concentration pattern is shown for a single random seed, leaving the stability of that pattern across runs unverified. H2 partially mitigates this risk by showing that two independent localization strategies converge on the same architectural regions for that seed, providing internal validation that the pattern is not a fluke of one selection rule. However, H2's credit does not address the multi-seed variance question—it uses the same single seed. The composition is thus partially unprotected: the convergent evidence strengthens the claim structurally, but the statistical uncertainty from P1 remains unresolved for this specific conclusion. The overall credibility is moderate-high because the convergent pattern is compelling, but a reader would need cross-seed evidence to fully credit the claim of consistent architectural concentration within the paper's own setup.

nodes.title: Localized weight differences concentrate in higher layers, predominantly the attention output dense layer

nodes.content: When using the subnetworks and localization masks to apply the local editing primitives (weight interpolation, weight extrapolation, pruning, mask switch) to a BERT-base-uncased target model with a reference of opposite gender-bias polarity (one stereotypical, one anti-stereotypical), the following results are obtained: (a) mask-based localization editing using a selected subset below 0.5% of all weights can effectively modify stereotypical gender bias as measured by the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT), StereoSet, and CrowS-Pairs; (b) varying the interpolation/extrapolation weighting factor $\alpha$ provides smooth and controllable shifts of bias between the target and reference regimes; and (c) for certain settings, WEAT indicates complete removal of the injected bias (introduced via Counterfactual Data Augmentation) at $\alpha=2$. These results show that very small, contrastively-chosen weight subsets suffice to control an intrinsic measure of gender stereotype encoded in BERT.

metadata.narrative: This conclusion is exposed on two fronts. P2 (measurement validity) is a high-necessity risk (p2=0.95): if the bias benchmarks do not validly measure the intended construct of gender stereotyping, the entire empirical evidence for bias control collapses into a claim about test scores. P3 (generalization) is a medium-necessity risk (p2=0.6): the approach is validated only for one architecture and injected bias, limiting its broader applicability. H3 provides substantial support within the tested regime by demonstrating reproducibility across seeds, sparsities, α values, and three measures, but H3's credit does not address the construct-validity challenge of P2, nor does it extend the conclusion beyond BERT-base and CDA. The composition is compounding: the measurement risk is entirely unprotected by any highlight, while the generalization risk is acknowledged but not resolved. The conclusion is credible for the narrow claim that the tested benchmarks can be systematically altered by editing tiny weight subsets in BERT-base with CDA-injected bias, but its interpretation as a general method for controlling real-world gender bias carries substantial and unresolved uncertainty.

nodes.title: Local contrastive editing on tiny subsets (<0.5%) can flexibly steer and remove measurable gender bias

nodes.content: As a control, applying the local editing primitives (weight interpolation, weight extrapolation, pruning, mask switch) to uninformed subsets of weights (randomly sampled from all weights except those pruned in both the stereotypical and anti-stereotypical BERT-base-uncased subnetworks) produces little or no change in the bias measures (WEAT, StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs), indicating that the localization step is critical: random tiny edits with the same cardinality do not reliably shift stereotypical gender associations.

metadata.narrative: H4 directly supports this conclusion through a well-designed control experiment that matches edit cardinality and editing primitives, showing that uninformed random edits produce minimal bias change. This guards against the alternative explanation that any small weight perturbation suffices to shift bias measures. No load-bearing weak points were identified because the control design is clean, the null result is clear across sparsities and α values, and the comparison fair. The conclusion is strongly supported within the experimental setup.

nodes.title: Localization is essential: uninformed/random edits have minimal effect on bias

nodes.content: Across the local editing strategies (interpolation, extrapolation, pruning, mask switch) and localization methods (mask-based, value-based) applied to BERT-base-uncased models, nearly all edits induce only minor increases in perplexity (masked language modeling) and minor downstream performance changes on the Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference (MNLI) and Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark (STS-B) tasks (maximum performance losses of at most ~1.07%/1.06% for most edits). The notable exception is value-based pruning, which causes large increases in perplexity (e.g., +9.529 at 30% sparsity) and significant drops in the language modeling (LM) score and downstream performance. Thus, local contrastive edits can be minimally invasive, but some primitives (value-based pruning of selected indices) can catastrophically damage language modeling ability.

metadata.narrative: P4 introduces a generalization risk: the performance evaluation covers perplexity, LM score, and two GLUE tasks, but leaves other capabilities (question answering, generation, factual recall) untested. H5 provides strong empirical support for the tested dimensions, with replication across seeds and sparsities and significance testing, establishing that mask-based and value-based interpolation/extrapolation are safe on those tasks while value-based pruning is harmful. The composition is partially unprotected: the safety claim for the tested tasks is well-evidenced, but the conclusion's implied generality (that most local edits preserve performance) is narrower than the tested suite. The exception of value-based pruning is clearly and robustly identified. The overall credibility is high for the tested tasks, with moderate uncertainty about unmeasured capabilities.

nodes.title: Most local edits preserve language modeling and downstream performance; value-based pruning is an exception that severely degrades performance

nodes.content: In sensitivity experiments for value-based interpolation (using the linear interpolation formula $\theta_t' = \theta_t + \alpha((\theta_r - \theta_t) \odot b)$ with a fixed weighting factor $\alpha=0.5$) on BERT-base-uncased subnetworks at 30% sparsity (stereotypical vs. anti-stereotypical), increasing the number $k$ of selected top-differing weights initially strengthens the effect on gender-bias measures (WEAT, StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs) up to a threshold of approximately 20–40% of candidate weights (the set of weights present in both subnetworks); beyond this range editing more weights yields little additional effect, indicating that a critical subset primarily encodes the gender-bias signal.

metadata.narrative: P5 identifies that the critical range (20-40%) was established at only one operational point: value-based interpolation with α=0.5. H6 provides strong, seed-averaged evidence of a plateau at this specific point across three bias measures, giving credence to the existence of a critical subset for that setting. The composition is bounded: the existence of a critical subset at α=0.5 is well-supported, but whether this threshold generalizes to other α values, extrapolation, or mask-based localization is an unprotected generalization risk. The conclusion as worded ("there exists a critical range... beyond which additional weights do not increase bias effects") is supported for the tested setting, but the practical recommendation to edit 20-40% of selected weights carries the hidden qualification that it applies only to value-based interpolation at α=0.5.

nodes.title: There exists a critical range (≈20–40%) of selected weights for value-based interpolation beyond which additional weights do not increase bias effects

nodes.content: Varying the interpolation/extrapolation factor $\alpha$ in local contrastive editing on BERT-base-uncased models yields monotonic increases in gender-bias-control effect size for moderate $|\alpha|$, providing a continuous calibration mechanism. However, for large absolute weighting factors ($|\alpha| \geq 5$), language modeling performance declines (increasing perplexity and decreasing language modeling (LM) score), and the bias effects become inconsistent. Thus, while $\alpha$ affords flexible control, there exists a practical operational range ($|\alpha| < 5$) beyond which edits harm model quality and reliability.

metadata.narrative: H7 directly supports this conclusion through a systematic α sweep that tracks three bias measures and perplexity across seeds, revealing both the monotonic control region and the breakdown at large |α|. No load-bearing weak points were identified because the empirical pattern is clear, the operational limits (|α|≥5) are explicitly identified and explained by concurrent perplexity increase, and the patent is replicated across seeds and localization strategies. The conclusion is well-supported for BERT-base with CDA injection, though the paper's limitation to one architecture and bias type implies that the specific operational range (|α| up to ~3) may not transfer directly to other models or bias specifications.

nodes.title: Effect magnitude correlates with weighting factor $\alpha$, but large $|\alpha|$ degrades language modeling (limits to extrapolation)

nodes.content: Applying local contrastive editing to a neutral BERT-base-uncased target model (fine-tuned on a subset of Wikipedia independent of the biased datasets constructed via Counterfactual Data Augmentation) shows that using the stereotypical reference model (fine-tuned on the stereotypical dataset) as the target can successfully steer the neutral model's gender bias in the expected direction (e.g., extrapolation with $\alpha=-2$ removes stereotypical bias per the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT)), while using an anti-stereotypical reference yields mixed results in some settings. These experiments indicate the method's applicability beyond parallel fine-tuning regimes (where target and reference are fine-tuned on similar data with opposite biases), but also expose limits when reference and target datasets differ.

metadata.narrative: This conclusion is inherently cautious, reporting both successful steering with a stereotypical reference (WEAT at α=-2) and mixed results with an anti-stereotypical reference. No load-bearing weak points were identified because the claim includes the mixed outcome as part of its conclusion rather than asserting a uniformly positive result. The paper acknowledges that dataset differences between target (neutral Wikipedia) and reference (CDA-fine-tuned) may confound localization. No distinguishing strength was identified beyond the effort to test wider applicability; the results are not uniformly positive and thus do not provide additional strong support for the method's generality, but they honestly characterize its limits. The conclusion is credible as reported: the method can work in some neutral-model settings but not reliably across all reference polarities.

nodes.title: Local contrastive editing can steer a neutral model using a stereotypical reference, but results with an anti-stereotypical reference are mixed

nodes.content: In the comparison of stereotypical and anti-stereotypical BERT-base-uncased subnetworks at 40% sparsity via both mask-based localization (selecting weights where pruning masks differ) and value-based localization (selecting top-k weights by absolute pruned-parameter difference), the fraction of selected weights per transformer component (attention query/value/key, attention output dense, intermediate dense, output dense) concentrates in the final layers (layers 8-11), with the maximum fraction in the attention output dense layer, as observed for one random seed.

metadata.failure_mode: If the architectural concentration pattern varies substantially across random seeds, then Conclusion 5's claim that localized weight differences concentrate in higher layers and the attention output dense layer loses the empirical support claimed by the paper. The intermediate step that fails is the extrapolation from a single-seed observation to a general property of the contrastive localization procedure. The scope of damage would be a narrowing from a confidently asserted architectural locus to an unverified trend, undermining the practical implication that edits can be structurally targeted to those components.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper presents the component-level selection distribution for a single random seed (Figure 3) without quantifying variance across the other three seeds used in the experiments. Given that iterative magnitude pruning can produce different pruning masks across seeds even with high Jaccard similarity, the distribution of selected weights per component may vary. The paper claims both strategies "consistently target similar areas", but this consistency claim rests on an unverified assumption about seed-invariance; the figure caption explicitly states "one random seed." The conclusion's reliance on this pattern for identifying architectural concentration is therefore based on an untested statistical stability.

nodes.title: Architectural localization shown for a single seed

nodes.content: In the evaluation of local contrastive editing on BERT-base-uncased models with injected binary gender stereotypes (via Counterfactual Data Augmentation), the three intrinsic bias measures used—the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT 8), the StereoSet intrasentence gender stereotype score, and the CrowS-Pairs gender stereotype score—serve as the operational definition of property p (gender stereotypical association). These benchmarks measure associations between fixed sets of target and attribute words (WEAT) or sentence-level stereotypical preferences (StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs) and have known construct-validity issues, including sensitivity to spurious corpus correlations, limited coverage of real-world gender associations, and reliance on a binary male/female specification that does not capture the full spectrum of gender identities. StereoSet and CrowS-Pairs have been criticized for methodological flaws.Blodgett et al., 2021; Pikuliak et al., 2023; Delobelle et al., 2022

metadata.failure_mode: If the benchmark scores do not validly measure the construct of gender stereotypical behavior (but instead capture artifacts of the injection or measurement setup), then the primary empirical evidence for Conclusion 6—that local contrastive editing can "effectively modify" and even "completely remove" gender bias—becomes unmoored from its intended referent. The concrete failure would be that the conclusion only reports changes in these specific benchmark scores, not in the socially relevant concept of bias that the paper's narrative invokes. The scope of damage is a fundamental narrowing: the claim of bias control reduces to a statement about performance on a few topic-specific tests, and the practical significance for fairness applications is unestablished.

refs.text: Blodgett et al., 2021; Pikuliak et al., 2023; Delobelle et al., 2022

metadata.weakness_reason: The paper uses three intrinsic bias benchmarks to measure the property of stereotypical gender bias. While triangulation across multiple measures is a standard practice, all three measures have been subject to critiques regarding their construct validity—whether they actually capture the intended social bias or confound it with other statistical properties of the data (e.g., frequency, sentiment). The WEAT 8 test in particular overlaps substantially with the terms used in the CDA injection, so changes in WEAT effect size may partly reflect direct shifts in token-level representations of the injected word pairs rather than a general change in stereotypical associations. The key uncertainty is whether reductions in these benchmark scores correspond to meaningful reductions in real-world gender stereotyping behavior of the model.

nodes.title: Validity of bias measurement benchmarks

nodes.content: The local contrastive editing experiments that demonstrate effective bias control are conducted exclusively on BERT-base-uncased (110 million parameters) with a single binary gender stereotype specification (male/female associations with stereotypical attribute words) injected via Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA) on subsets of English Wikipedia. The approach is not tested on other model families (GPT, T5, LLaMA), larger models, non-binary gender biases, other social biases (race, age, religion), or on naturally occurring (non-injected) biases present in pretrained models without explicit CDA.

metadata.failure_mode: If the method's success is contingent on properties of the BERT-base architecture, the CDA injection scheme, or the specific binary gender specification, then Conclusion 6's claim of having demonstrated a "parameter-efficient, minimally invasive bias-control method" is valid only for a narrow regime. The concrete loss is that practitioners seeking to apply the method to other models (e.g., generative LLMs) or other bias types (e.g., racial stereotypes) lack any evidence from this paper for its effectiveness. The scope of damage is a substantial narrowing of the conclusion's implied generality, bringing it from a broadly claimed feasibility to a proof-of-concept in one controlled setting.
metadata.weakness_reason: The injection-based setup creates a controlled but highly artificial environment where target and reference models differ only in the swapped target terms and the MLM fine-tuning data is identical except for these swaps. In realistic settings, biases arise from multiple interacting corpus properties, and the contrastive signal between a neutral and a biased model may be diffused across many data-driven differences. The paper explicitly acknowledges these limitations in Section 7, but the abstract and introduction present the method as a general approach for controlling stereotypical bias in language models, implying broader applicability. The computational cost of iterative magnitude pruning further limits practical extension to larger models, as noted in Appendix B.

nodes.title: Generalization beyond the tested architecture and bias injection

nodes.content: The evaluation of how local contrastive editing preserves language modeling performance on BERT-base-uncased models uses perplexity (masked language modeling), language modeling (LM) score (StereoSet meaningfulness), and two downstream tasks from the GLUE benchmark: Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference (MNLI) and Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark (STS-B). Other common capabilities such as question answering (e.g., SQuAD), factual recall, open-ended generation, robustness to adversarial inputs, and zero-shot or few-shot performance are not assessed.

metadata.failure_mode: If tasks not tested (e.g., question answering, factual recall, open-ended generation) suffer substantial degradation after editing, the conclusion that the edits "largely preserve a model's language modeling ability and downstream task performance" would be misleading: the edits might be only safe for sentence-pair classification tasks but harmful for generative or retrieval tasks. The concrete loss would be that the paper's practical recommendation to practitioners (use interpolation, avoid value-based pruning) would be insufficiently informed by the narrow evaluation. The scope of damage is a narrowing of the safety claim from "most local edits preserve performance" to "most local edits preserve performance on sentence-level classification benchmarks and perplexity."
metadata.weakness_reason: While perplexity and two GLUE tasks are standard benchmarks for evaluating language model quality, they do not cover the full range of capabilities a language model may be deployed for. The paper's claim that "most local edits preserve language modeling and downstream performance" and that "edited models can still be effectively used in downstream tasks" is explicitly tied to MNLI and STS-B. The absence of evaluation on a more diverse task set leaves open the possibility of significant degradation in unmeasured capabilities, particularly for tasks that more heavily rely on verbatim recall or generation fluency. The LM score partially addresses meaningfulness but on a single dataset (StereoSet) that has its own validity issues.

nodes.title: Performance preservation evaluated on a limited task set

nodes.content: The sensitivity analysis establishing a critical range of 20-40% of selected weights as the threshold beyond which additional selected weights do not increase bias effects is performed exclusively for value-based interpolation (linear interpolation formula $\theta_t' = \theta_t + \alpha((\theta_r - \theta_t) \odot b)$) with a fixed weighting factor $\alpha=0.5$, on BERT-base-uncased subnetworks at 30% sparsity, with results shown for three bias measures (WEAT, StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs) across four random seeds. The analysis does not test whether the same threshold holds for other $\alpha$ values (e.g., $\alpha=0.2$, $\alpha=0.8$, or extrapolation $\alpha>1$), for mask-based localization, or for other sparsity levels of the subnetworks.

metadata.failure_mode: If the critical range depends on α or the localization strategy, then Conclusion 9's claim that there exists a single critical range (20-40%) of selected weights for value-based interpolation is an oversimplification of a more complex interaction. The practical recommendation that editing 20-40% of candidate weights is sufficient would be misleading for settings with different α values or for mask-based editing. The concrete failure is that practitioners applying the method at α≠0.5 would not know whether the same range applies, and the paper does not supply the evidence to guide that decision. The scope of damage is a narrowing from a general empirical law (the critical subset idea) to a single-slice observation.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper infers that there exists a critical subset of weights primarily encoding the bias signal, but this inference is drawn from a single operational point (α=0.5 for value-based interpolation). The effect of varying the number of selected weights k may interact with α: at larger α, even a few weights might saturate the effect; at smaller α, more weights may be needed. Similarly, mask-based localization might not exhibit the same saturation pattern because it selects a different set of weights (those pruned in one subnetwork but not the other) rather than the top-difference weights. The paper does not present evidence for the threshold's invariance across these dimensions.

nodes.title: Critical range tested only at one weighting factor for one localization strategy

nodes.content: For both stereotypical and anti-stereotypical BERT-base-uncased models fine-tuned with Counterfactual Data Augmentation on English Wikipedia, iterative magnitude pruning yields subnetworks at sparsities up to 40% whose pruning masks have a Jaccard similarity greater than 0.98 across four random seeds, and whose biases measured by the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT), StereoSet stereotype score, and CrowS-Pairs stereotype score remain within a few percentage points of the full-model biases across all sparsity levels (10%, 20%, 30%, 40%) as shown in Table 1.

metadata.credit: This strength guards against the failure that the subnetworks used for localization are unstable artifacts of a specific random seed or that they lose the bias signal needed for contrastive comparison. The high mask similarity across seeds (Jaccard >0.98) shows that iterative magnitude pruning discovers a consistent subnetwork structure independent of initialization or training order, making the pruning masks reliable for cross-model comparisons across different seeds. The bias-preservation evidence, measured by three independent bias instruments, ensures that the subnetworks carry the same behavioral signature of gender stereotyping as their parent models, which is essential for the subsequent localization step where opposite-polarity subnetworks are compared. Without this stability and preservation, the entire localization-and-editing pipeline would rest on unreliable foundations; with this evidence, the conclusion that subnetworks are valid inputs for contrastive editing is directly and substantially underwritten.

nodes.title: Stable subnetworks with preserved bias across seeds and measures

nodes.content: In the comparison of stereotypical and anti-stereotypical BERT-base-uncased subnetworks at 40% sparsity, the mask-based localization strategy (Equation 1, selecting weights where pruning masks differ between subnetworks) and the value-based localization strategy (Equation 2, selecting top-k weights with largest absolute differences in pruned parameter values) produce selection distributions across transformer components (attention query/value/key, attention output dense, intermediate dense, output dense) that both peak in the final encoder layers (layers 8-11 of the 12-layer BERT) and show the largest fractions of selected weights in the attention output dense (feed-forward projection) layer, as illustrated in Figure 3 for one random seed.

metadata.credit: This convergent pattern guards against the failure that either localization strategy identifies architecturally irrelevant weights due to its specific design (e.g., mask-based selection may pick up arbitrary pruning differences stemming from CDA data ordering, value-based selection may pick up unrelated numerical variations that happen to differ between the two finetuned models). Two fundamentally different selection principles—one based on binary presence in the subnetwork structure, the other on the magnitude of value differences in shared weights—independently pointing to the same architectural regions provides strong evidence that those regions are genuinely implicated in the stereotype encoding, rather than being artifacts of a single selection rule. The layer of credibility underwritten is the attribution of the bias signal to higher-layer attention output dense components; without this convergence, the attribution could be dismissed as a quirk of the localization procedure. The scope of credit is that the conclusion's architectural localization claim gains internal validation that a single strategy alone could not provide.

nodes.title: Convergent evidence from two independent localization strategies

nodes.content: The effects of local contrastive editing on gender bias are evaluated across four random seeds for both target-reference directions (stereotypical-to-anti-stereotypical and anti-stereotypical-to-stereotypical), at multiple sparsity levels (10%, 20%, 30%, 40%), and for weighting factors α ranging from -5 to 5, with bias measured by three instruments: the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT) effect size, the StereoSet stereotype score, and the CrowS-Pairs stereotype score. Per-point means and standard deviations are reported (Figure 4, Figure 6). Perplexity and LM score changes are tested for statistical significance using a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Bonferroni correction at each sparsity level (Table 5).

metadata.credit: This extensive characterization guards against the failure that observed bias changes are artifacts of a particular random seed, sparsity level, or measurement instrument. The four-seed averaging with error bars provides quantitative evidence of reproducibility across runs. The use of three partially independent bias measures shows that the editing effect is not a single-benchmark artifact—the trends are broadly consistent across WEAT, StereoSet, and CrowS-Pairs. The systematic α sweep demonstrates controllability (monotonic change for moderate |α|) and identifies the breakdown at large |α|. The significance testing on perplexity and LM score changes separates genuine degradation from chance variation. Together, these elements underwrite the conclusion that local contrastive editing can reliably and flexibly steer measured bias across multiple experimental conditions; without them, the claim would rest on single-point comparisons with unquantified variation.

nodes.title: Multi-seed, multi-measure, multi-α empirical characterization with error bars and significance testing

nodes.content: When the same editing primitives (weight interpolation, extrapolation, pruning) are applied to randomly sampled subsets of BERT-base-uncased weights (excluding those already pruned in both the target and reference subnetworks) with the cardinality matched exactly to the number of weights selected by the localization strategies, the resulting changes in the Word Embedding Association Test, StereoSet, and CrowS-Pairs bias measures are minimal across all sparsity levels and α values, as shown in Figure 4 for 30% sparsity and in the supplementary results for other sparsities.

metadata.credit: This control directly guards against the failure that any small set of weight changes, regardless of principled selection, can alter bias measurements—which would undermine the need for the localization step as a methodological contribution. By matching the number of edited weights and using the same editing primitives, the comparison isolates the effect of principled localization from the effect of arbitrary perturbation. The null result for uninformed edits across multiple sparsities and α values provides strong comparative evidence that the observed bias changes in conditioned edits are not due to random perturbation but specifically to the localization procedure. The layer of credibility underwritten is the causal attribution: the localization step is necessary for bias control. Without this control, the claim that localization is essential would be speculative; with it, the conclusion is directly supported by a well-designed experiment that rules out the trivial alternative.

nodes.title: Uninformed editing control with matched cardinality directly establishes localization necessity

nodes.content: Performance of edited BERT-base-uncased models is evaluated using perplexity (masked language modeling), the StereoSet language modeling score (meaningfulness), and two GLUE benchmark downstream tasks: MNLI (multi-genre natural language inference, reporting matched and mismatched accuracy) and STS-B (semantic textual similarity, reporting Pearson and Spearman correlation). The evaluation is conducted across four random seeds, at multiple sparsity levels (10%, 20%, 30%, 40%), and for both localization strategies (mask-based and value-based). Changes in perplexity and LM score are tested for significance using a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Bonferroni correction (Table 5). Results in Tables 2, 5, 6, and 7 show that mask-based editing and value-based interpolation/extrapolation incur at most approximately 0.07 perplexity increase and less than 1.1% downstream performance loss, while value-based pruning consistently causes large degradation (perplexity increase of approximately 9-12 points and LM score drop of approximately 2-3 points).

metadata.credit: This evaluation safeguards against the failure that editing silently degrades unmeasured core capabilities that would make the model unusable despite successful bias modification. By testing on two linguistically distinct downstream tasks (NLI requires understanding of entailment; STS-B requires fine-grained semantic similarity) plus direct language modeling metrics (perplexity and LM score), the paper provides broad empirical coverage of the model's functionality. The significance testing on perplexity and LM score changes distinguishes real degradation from chance fluctuations. The replication across four seeds and multiple sparsity levels shows that the preservation pattern is robust, not a single lucky run. The exception of value-based pruning is reliably identified as a harmful operation. The layer of credibility underwritten is the quantitative assertion that most local edits are minimally invasive across the tested dimensions; without this evaluation, the safety claim would be unsupported, and with it, practitioners have evidence-backed guidance on which operations to use.

nodes.title: Comprehensive performance evaluation with significance testing and replication across sparsities

nodes.content: In the sensitivity analysis for value-based interpolation on BERT-base-uncased subnetworks at 30% sparsity with weighting factor α=0.5, the number k of selected top-differing weights (by absolute pruned-parameter difference) is varied from 0 to 100% of the candidate set. The Word Embedding Association Test effect size, StereoSet stereotype score, and CrowS-Pairs stereotype score are plotted with means and standard deviations across four random seeds (Figure 5). The curves show a steep initial change from 0% to approximately 20% of candidates, a plateau between 20% and 40%, and no further change beyond 40%.

metadata.credit: This analysis guards against the failure that the effect of value-based interpolation varies arbitrarily with the number of weights selected without saturation, which would leave the notion of a "critical subset" ungrounded and provide no guidance for practitioners on how many weights to edit. The plateau across three bias measures with quantified seed variance provides clear, reproducible evidence that beyond a threshold, additional high-difference weights do not contribute further bias change. The layer of credibility underwritten is the existence of a concentrated signal within the candidate set; without this sweep, the optimal k would be unknown and the efficiency claim that a tiny subset suffices would be weaker. The scope of credit is strong empirical grounding of the threshold for the tested setting (α=0.5, value-based), making the claim about a critical subset quantitatively supported rather than speculative.

nodes.title: Systematic k sensitivity analysis with seed averaging reveals a clear plateau

nodes.content: On BERT-base-uncased subnetworks at 30% sparsity, the weighting factor α for contrastive editing (interpolation: α in [0,1]; extrapolation: α outside [0,1]) is varied from -5 to 5 for both mask-based and value-based localization, with the Word Embedding Association Test effect size, StereoSet stereotype score, CrowS-Pairs stereotype score, and perplexity change measured across four random seeds. The results (Figure 6) show monotonic bias change for |α| up to approximately 3, increasing perplexity for large |α|, and inconsistency in the StereoSet and CrowS-Pairs measures for |α|≥5.

metadata.credit: This α sweep guards against the failure that the weighting factor has no systematic effect on bias, or that it degrades model performance before achieving meaningful bias control, which would negate the usefulness of α as a calibration knob. By simultaneously tracking three bias measures and perplexity across multiple seeds, the experiment reveals both the controllability region (monotonic bias change for |α| up to ~3) and the breakdown point (inconsistency and perplexity increase at |α|≥5), providing a practical operating range. The monotonic trend in WEAT confirms the editing's directionality, while the divergence of StereoSet/CrowS-Pairs at large |α|—indicating inconsistent model behavior—is explained by the concurrent perplexity increase. Without this sweep, the claim that α provides a continuous control knob would be unchecked; with it, both the existence of controllable modulation and its empirical limits are thoroughly characterized.

nodes.title: Systematic α sweep across three bias measures and perplexity reveals operational range

steps.reasoning: Define the overall localization goal and the subnetwork notation. The aim is to identify individual weights associated with a property of interest $p$ by comparing a target subnetwork $f_t(\cdot, m_t \odot \theta_t)$ and a reference subnetwork $f_r(\cdot, m_r \odot \theta_r)$, where $m_t, m_r \in \{0,1\}^d$ are binary pruning masks, $\theta_t, \theta_r \in \mathbb{R}^d$ are parameter vectors, and $\odot$ denotes element-wise product. A localization mask $b \in \{0,1\}^d$ is defined from an index set $\mathcal{I} \subseteq \{1,\dots,d\}$ by $b_i = \mathbb{1}\{i \in \mathcal{I}\}$, so $b_i=1$ indicates that weight index $i$ is selected for editing.

Define mask-based localization formally and state the authors' hypothesis for why this selection captures information about $p$. Given pruning masks $m_t$ and $m_r$ for the target and reference subnetworks, compute the localization mask $b$ as
$$
b = m_t \odot m_r.
$$
The authors state the hypothesis that weights present in one subnetwork but not the other (i.e. differences in pruning masks) likely encode information relevant to the property $p$ because a weight's presence/absence differs between subnetworks specialized for differing properties.
Figure 2
Chen et al. (2020)

Define value-based localization formally, including the index set construction and the selection rule. Compute the element-wise absolute difference between the pruned parameter vectors,
$$
\big|(m_r \odot \theta_r) - (m_t \odot \theta_t)\big|,
$$
then let $I_{top}^k$ be the index set containing the indices of the $k$ largest entries of this absolute-difference vector. Define the localization mask $b$ by
$$
b_i =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } i \in I_{top}^k,\\[6pt]
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
The authors hypothesize that weights with the largest absolute differences are those that most strongly steer the networks toward opposing directions with respect to the property $p$.
Figure 2

Connect these two strategies to the broader experimental workflow. The authors operationalize fine-grained localization of weights that will be edited in subsequent contrastive editing steps by producing $b$ via either mask-based or value-based localization; these localization masks then restrict application of the editing primitives (interpolation, extrapolation, pruning, mask switch) to localized coordinates.

Define the editing problem setting and all symbols used. Let $f(x,\theta)$ denote the output of a neural network with parameters $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d$ for input $x$, where $d$ is the number of scalar parameters. Let $f_t(\cdot,\theta_t)$ be the target network with parameter vector $\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$, let $f_r(\cdot,\theta_r)$ be the reference network with parameter vector $\theta_r \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and let $b \in \{0,1\}^d$ be a localization mask with elements $b_i = 1$ indicating indices selected for editing. The goal is to produce an edited parameter vector $\theta_t'$ that differs from $\theta_t$ only at indices where $b_i=1$.

Present the weight interpolation (IP) primitive, including symbol definitions and domain of the interpolation coefficient. Define the scalar weighting factor $\alpha$ and specify its domain for interpolation. The weight interpolation primitive modifies $\theta_t$ only at indices selected by $b$ according to the equation
$$
\theta_t' = \theta_t + \alpha\big((\theta_r - \theta_t) \odot b\big),
\quad \alpha \in [0,1],
$$
where $\odot$ denotes element-wise product (Hadamard product). Here $\alpha = 0$ leaves the target unchanged and $\alpha = 1$ fully adopts the reference values on the selected indices.
Ilharco et al. (2022a); Wortsman et al. (2022); Yadav et al. (2024)

Present the weight extrapolation (EP) primitive as a generalization of interpolation, specifying the allowed domain for $\alpha$ and its semantic effect. Using the same symbols as above, define extrapolation by
$$
\theta_t' = \theta_t + \alpha\big((\theta_r - \theta_t) \odot b\big),
\quad \alpha \in \mathbb{R}\setminus[0,1].
$$
This allows moving selected weights beyond the reference values or in the opposite direction when $\alpha$ is outside $[0,1]$.

Present the pruning (PR) primitive and define its effect and symbols. Pruning zeroes the selected coordinates of $\theta_t$ by
$$
\theta_t' = \theta_t - (\theta_t \odot b),
$$
which is equivalent to setting $\theta_{t,i}' = 0$ for every index $i$ with $b_i = 1$ and leaving other coordinates unchanged.

Present the mask switch (SW) primitive, state its precondition (applicability only with mask-based localization), and define the operation precisely. Let $m_r \in \{0,1\}^d$ be the reference pruning mask (so $m_{r,i}=1$ indicates that the $i$-th parameter is retained in the reference subnetwork). The mask switch operation applies the reference subnetwork mask to the target:
$$
\theta_t' = \theta_t \odot m_r.
$$
This operation both prunes target parameters where $m_{r,i}=0$ and restores (keeps) parameters where $m_{r,i}=1$, and is explicitly applicable when localization was performed via pruning masks.

Emphasize the locality constraint and contrastive nature of the defined primitives. Each primitive is explicitly restricted to indices with $b_i = 1$, i.e. the edit modifies only a small, localized subset of coordinates identified by a localization strategy; this enforces parameter-efficient, contrastive edits that operate relative to a chosen reference model.

State the experimental setting used to discover subnetworks and define symbols. Use iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) on fine-tuned BERT models. Let $f(\cdot,\theta)$ be a pre-trained network and IMP operate by alternating fine-tuning for $i$ steps and globally pruning a fixed proportion $p\%$ of weights of lowest magnitude, producing a pruning mask $m \in \{0,1\}^d$ and a subnetwork $f(\cdot, m \odot \theta)$. After pruning, remaining weights are reset to initial values and the procedure repeats until a target sparsity is reached. The authors set the per-iteration pruning rate to $p\% = 10\%$.
Chen et al. (2020)

Define the criterion used to accept a subnetwork as a "winning ticket" and state the applied evaluation protocol. A subnetwork is accepted as a winning ticket if its performance after the designated fine-tuning steps $i$ is within $5\%$ of the performance of the full model fine-tuned for the same number of steps. The authors applied this criterion when extracting subnetworks from fine-tuned BERT models.

Report the empirical discovery: subnetworks up to 40% sparsity satisfy the winning-ticket criterion on fine-tuned BERT. The authors applied IMP to stereotypical and anti-stereotypical fine-tuned BERT models and discovered subnetworks at multiple sparsity levels up to 40% that meet the stated winning-ticket performance threshold.
Table 1

Report stability of the discovered subnetworks across random seeds and how this was measured. The authors ran the IMP procedure across four different random seeds and measured the Jaccard similarity of the resulting pruning masks $m$ across runs. They observed Jaccard similarity values greater than $0.98$, indicating that the subnetworks are highly stable across seeds.

Report that the discovered subnetworks largely maintain the bias of their parent models and identify the bias evaluation measures. Using intrinsic bias benchmarks (the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT), StereoSet (SS), and CrowS-Pairs (CS)), the authors measured the bias of both full models and their extracted subnetworks at different sparsity levels and reported that the subnetworks largely preserve the stereotypical or anti-stereotypical bias of the parent models. The bias values for subnetworks at multiple sparsity levels are reported as means across random seeds in the paper's Table 1.
Table 1
Caliskan et al. (2017); Nadeem et al. (2020); Nangia et al. (2020)

Start from the established upstream result that subnetworks were discovered via iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) and are stable winning tickets up to 40% sparsity with highly similar masks across seeds (this is treated as known from the earlier conclusion regarding IMP-extracted subnetworks and their properties).

Describe the empirical comparison used to quantify mask differences between stereotypical and anti-stereotypical subnetworks. The authors compared the pruning masks $m$ of subnetworks extracted from the stereotypical and anti-stereotypical models at multiple sparsity levels (from 10% up to 40%), computing the percentage of parameter indices at which the two masks differ.

Report the observed quantitative result and its interpretation. Across all evaluated sparsity levels, the authors observed that the percentage of weights where the pruning masks differ remained below $0.5\%$. From this they infer that the two subnetworks are highly similar overall and that parameter differences correlated with the injected stereotypical vs. anti-stereotypical signals are concentrated in a very small fraction of indices.
Figure 3

Start from the known facts established earlier: (a) the localization strategies (mask-based and value-based) are formally defined (treat conclusion 1 as known), and (b) IMP-extracted subnetworks exist for stereotypical and anti-stereotypical models up to 40% sparsity and are available for comparison (treat conclusion 3 as known).

Describe the application of both localization strategies to the pair of subnetworks and the measurement performed. The authors applied mask-based localization (comparing pruning masks) and value-based localization (selecting top-$k$ absolute differences of pruned parameter vectors) to the stereotypical vs. anti-stereotypical subnetworks and recorded which architectural components and layers are selected by each strategy.

Report the observed architectural concentration and where localized indices predominantly occur. Both localization strategies consistently concentrated their selected indices in the higher layers of the transformer, with a pronounced focus on the attention output dense layers (the projection/feed-forward components following attention) in the last layers of the network. The authors note that the selected indices are not randomly distributed but instead cluster in specific higher-layer components.
Figure 3

Connect the observation to prior literature cited by the authors. The authors relate this architectural concentration to prior work that found influential attention components for gender bias in higher layers, thereby aligning their localization findings with previous studies indicating higher-layer localization of bias.
Ma et al. (2023); Chintam et al. (2023); Vig et al. (2020)

Treat as known the following upstream results: (i) localization strategies that produce masks $b$ identifying small sets of indices (conclusion 1), (ii) local editing primitives (interpolation, extrapolation, pruning, mask switch) that operate on indices where $b_i=1$ (conclusion 2), and (iii) the availability of stereotypical and anti-stereotypical subnetworks extracted via IMP (conclusion 3). These are the starting premises for the experiments described in the paper's evaluation of edits.

Describe the experiment configuration used to test bias steering: the authors used stereotypical subnetworks as one polarity and anti-stereotypical subnetworks as the opposite polarity; they formed target/reference pairs by choosing a target model with one polarity and the reference with the opposite polarity; they applied localization to obtain $b$ (mask-based or value-based) and then applied edits (IP, EP, PR, SW) restricted to indices with $b_i=1$; they evaluated bias with WEAT, StereoSet (SS), and CrowS-Pairs (CS) averaged across four random seeds.
Figure 4

Report the principal empirical finding about tiny mask-based edits (<0.5% of weights) and their effectiveness on intrinsic bias measures. The authors observed that mask-based editing using a selected subset below $0.5\%$ of all weights can effectively modify stereotypical gender bias as measured by WEAT, StereoSet and CrowS-Pairs. This claim is supported by reported results showing measurable shifts in these metrics when applying edits to localized subsets of this size.
Figure 4
Table 1

Report the finding about controllability via the interpolation/extrapolation weighting factor $\alpha$. By varying the weighting factor $\alpha$ in interpolation/extrapolation operations, the authors observed smooth and controllable shifts of bias between the target and the reference regimes (WEAT shows continuous changes as $\alpha$ varies). Specifically, the paper reports that for certain settings WEAT indicates complete removal of the injected bias at $\alpha = 2$ (i.e., extrapolation with that magnitude yields a WEAT effect size consistent with neutralization in those experiments).
Figure 6

State the overall interpretation: combining localized masks derived from contrastive subnetworks with local editing primitives permits steering and removal of measurable gender bias using very small contrastively-chosen subsets (below 0.5% of weights), demonstrating that tiny, targeted edits suffice to control an intrinsic measure of gender stereotyping encoded in BERT.

Treat as known the localization strategies and editing primitives (conclusions 1 and 2): localization produces a mask $b$ identifying selected indices, and editing primitives change only coordinates with $b_i=1$. Also state the uninformed editing sampling procedure used as a control: for uninformed interpolation/extrapolation the authors randomly sampled weights from all weights excluding those pruned in both subnetworks; for uninformed pruning they randomly sampled weights present in the target subnetwork excluding already-pruned ones; in each case the number of sampled weights equalled the cardinality of the localized mask to ensure a fair comparison.
Figure 4

Describe the empirical control experiment and the observed outcome. The authors applied the same editing primitives (IP, EP, PR) to these uninformed random subsets and measured changes in bias using WEAT, StereoSet and CrowS-Pairs. They observed little or no change in bias measures when editing uninformed random subsets of the same cardinality, indicating that random tiny edits do not reliably shift stereotypical associations.
Figure 4

Interpretation: because the uninformed edits match the localized edits in size but produce negligible bias change, localization is essential — the effectiveness of the local contrastive editing approach derives from choosing contrastive, property-relevant coordinates rather than from merely editing a small number of parameters.

Cite the methodological description of uninformed editing to justify the control's fairness. The uninformed editing procedure was explicitly designed to exclude weights pruned in both subnetworks (so that interpolation/extrapolation could affect them) and to match the localized subset sizes, ensuring the observed difference in effect is attributable to localization rather than subset cardinality.
Chen et al. (2020)

Treat as known the editing primitives (conclusion 2) and the set of localization strategies (conclusion 1). State the evaluation metrics used to measure language modeling and downstream performance: perplexity as primary LM measure, the LM score (StereoSet LM metric) as a secondary LM measure, and downstream task metrics (MNLI matched/mismatched accuracy; STS-B Pearson/Spearman correlation). Authors also report mean changes across seeds and highlight statistically significant increases in perplexity or drops in LM score.
Table 2

Report the general empirical observation about invasiveness of edits on language modeling and downstream tasks. The authors report that nearly all editing strategies induced only minor increases in perplexity and minor downstream performance changes, with maximum reported performance losses of at most approximately $1.07\%$/$1.06\%$ for STS-B and at most $0.71\%$/$0.59\%$ for MNLI across the reported edits (these numbers are taken from Table 2 reporting downstream performance after edits).
Table 2

Identify and quantify the notable exception: value-based pruning severely degrades language modeling ability. From the experiments the authors report that value-based pruning causes large increases in perplexity — for example, Table 5 reports an average perplexity increase of $+9.529$ at 30% sparsity (this value appears in the table of mean changes in perplexity after value-based pruning). The same table shows substantial LM score drops (e.g., $-2.723$ points at 30% sparsity), and downstream task evaluations (Table 2 and appendix tables) show the largest task performance drops occur for value-based pruning.
Table 5

Conclude the authors' interpretation: local contrastive edits are largely minimally invasive to language modeling and downstream performance, but the particular primitive of value-based pruning (i.e. zeroing the selected top-$k$ differing parameters) can catastrophically damage language modeling ability and thereby impair bias evaluation or downstream utility.

Treat the localization strategies and editing primitives as known (conclusions 1 and 2). Define the experimental variable under study: for value-based localization, the number $k$ of selected top-differing weights is varied and the effect on bias measures is recorded; the specific interpolation setting considered in this sensitivity experiment uses $\alpha = 0.5$.

Describe the empirical sweep and how effects are quantified. The authors performed experiments varying $k$ (expressed either as absolute counts or as percentages of candidate weights) and measured the bias-change effects (e.g., WEAT effect size) and changes in perplexity averaged across seeds and both target polarities. Figure 5 reports the sensitivity results for value-based interpolation with $\alpha = 0.5$ at sparsity 30% averaged across four random seeds.
Figure 5

Report the observed threshold behavior and its interpretation. Increasing $k$ initially strengthens the observed effect on gender-bias measures up to a threshold of approximately $20\%$–$40\%$ of candidate weights; beyond this range editing additional weights yields little or no additional effect on the bias measures. The authors interpret this as evidence that a critical, smaller subset primarily encodes the bias signal, so editing beyond that subset produces diminishing returns.

Note secondary observations about side effects on perplexity for these $k$ variations. The authors report that across the choices of $k$ explored in Figure 5 there was no significant increase in perplexity on average, indicating that the observed plateau in bias effect size is not explained by gross degradation of language modeling ability for larger $k$ in these experiments.
Figure 5

Treat as known the editing primitives (conclusion 2) and the evaluation metrics (perplexity, LM score, WEAT, StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs). Define the experimental variable: the interpolation/extrapolation weighting factor $\alpha$ is varied over a range of values (including moderate magnitudes and large magnitudes such as $|\alpha| \ge 5$), and bias and language-modeling metrics are recorded.

Describe the empirical trend for moderate $|\alpha|$: the authors report that increasing the absolute value of $\alpha$ for interpolation/extrapolation produces monotonic increases in the effect size on WEAT (i.e. bias-control magnitude increases smoothly with higher $|\alpha|$ within a moderate range). Figure 6 (bias plots) illustrates smooth, monotonous change in WEAT as $\alpha$ is varied.
Figure 6

Describe the empirical adverse effects for large $|\alpha|$ and the observed threshold where behavior breaks down. For large absolute weighting factors (the authors report inconsistencies and degradation for $|\alpha| \ge 5$), language modeling performance declines (evidenced by increasing perplexity in the perplexity plots and decreasing LM scores), and the bias effects become inconsistent across seeds and settings. The paper cites increasing perplexity in Figure 6b and supplementary figures 17 and 18 as evidence that very large $|\alpha|$ harm overall model quality and reliability.
Figure 6
Figure 17
Figure 18

Conclude the practical implication: while the weighting factor $\alpha$ affords continuous calibration of bias-control magnitude (monotonic for moderate $|\alpha|$), there exists a practical operational range for $\alpha$ beyond which edits damage language modeling ability and produce inconsistent bias outcomes; thus extrapolation is limited by language-modeling degradation at large $|\alpha|$.

State the new experimental setting and define symbols: a neutral target model is fine-tuned on a dataset independent of the biased (stereotypical/anti-stereotypical) datasets; from this neutral model the authors extract neutral subnetworks at different sparsities with four random seeds (symbols: neutral target subnetwork $f_{neutral}(\cdot,m_{neutral}\odot\theta_{neutral})$, reference subnetworks stereotypical or anti-stereotypical $f_{stereo}$/$f_{anti}$).

Describe how localization and editing are applied in this cross-dataset scenario. The authors compute localization masks by comparing the neutral subnetworks to a reference subnetwork (either stereotypical or anti-stereotypical) using the same mask-based or value-based localization procedures, then apply local contrastive edits (e.g., extrapolation with specified $\alpha$ values) restricted to the localized indices and evaluate bias with WEAT (and complementary measures).
Figure 7

Report the empirical outcome when using a stereotypical reference: editing the neutral model with a stereotypical reference can steer the neutral model's bias in the expected (stereotypical) direction; the authors provide the specific example that extrapolation with $\alpha = -2$ successfully removes stereotypical bias as measured by WEAT in their experiments (i.e., WEAT indicates the neutral model becomes less stereotypical under that edit).
Figure 7

Report the empirical outcome when using an anti-stereotypical reference and provide the authors' interpretation of mixed results. When using an anti-stereotypical reference to edit the neutral model, the authors observed mixed and sometimes inconclusive results: in some scenarios the neutral model's bias shifted as expected toward anti-stereotypical associations, while in others the change was weaker or inconsistent. The authors interpret this as a consequence of the datasets differing (the reference and neutral target were fine-tuned on disjoint datasets), so localized weights may encode dataset differences beyond stereotypical bias and thereby produce less consistent steering.
Figure 7

Summarize applicability and limits: local contrastive editing can be applied beyond parallel fine-tuning regimes (i.e., to neutral targets versus biased references), but the success depends on how exclusively the localized weights encode the target property versus other dataset-specific signals; when the reference and target datasets differ, results may be mixed and require further investigation.

open_questions.content: Remaining unresolved scientific issues and limitations acknowledged by the authors: (1) Generalization across architectures and bias types: experiments were conducted on a single architecture (BERT-base-uncased) and a single binary gender-bias specification; it remains untested whether the localization and editing procedures, the small-fraction effect sizes, and the safe operational ranges of $\alpha$ transfer to other model families, larger models, or non-binary and other social bias specifications. (2) Causal interpretation and specificity: although localized indices correlate with measured stereotype changes, the causal mechanisms by which those individual weights produce stereotype-bearing behavior are not fully characterized; disentangling dataset-induced differences from genuine stereotype encodings (especially when editing neutral models with non-overlapping data) requires further analysis. (3) Limits of extrapolation and edit magnitude: the experiments identify practical ranges for $\alpha$ beyond which language modeling degrades, but a principled understanding of these limits (e.g., why $|\alpha|\geq 5$ leads to inconsistency) and how they scale with model size and sparsity is open. (4) Safety and dual-use concerns: the same local editing machinery can be used to amplify or introduce biases, and the ethical and governance questions around releasing such tools and safeguards remain unresolved. (5) Computational cost and feasibility: iterative magnitude pruning and the extraction of stable subnetworks required substantial compute (detailed in Appendix B); more efficient subnetwork discovery or localization algorithms are needed to make the approach practical at larger scales.
